readerTitle: How WorldCom turned $3.8 billion of phone bills into 'investments'
caseNote: 실제 기업 (WorldCom, 2002년 회계 부정) + 가상 적용 (사내 운영팀, 매장 12곳의 소매 체인) · 계산 수치는 설명용
insight: 같은 돈을 써도 자산으로 기록하느냐 비용으로 기록하느냐에 따라 올해 이익이 달라진다. 기준은 '다음 해에도 이 지출이 사업에 도움이 되는가'이고, 현금은 어느 쪽이든 똑같이 나간다.
misconception: 지출을 자산으로 기록하면 돈을 아낀 것이거나 사업이 더 좋아진 것이다. 자산과 비용의 구분은 회계 담당자의 형식일 뿐이다.

sources.text: WorldCom press release, June 25, 2002: announcement that about $3.8 billion of line costs had been improperly recorded as capital expenditures
U.S. SEC v. WorldCom, Inc., complaint filed June 26, 2002
Report of Investigation by the Special Investigative Committee of the Board of Directors of WorldCom, Inc. (Beresford, Katzenbach & Rogers, 2003)
자산·비용 구분은 재무회계의 표준 개념. 4·7·8번 카드의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: WorldCom이 2002년 6월 25일에 약 38억 달러의 회선 비용(line costs)을 자본적 지출로 잘못 기록했다고 발표한 내용을 1차 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
내부감사팀(Cynthia Cooper 주도)이 문제를 찾아낸 경위와, 2002년 7월 파산 신청 시점을 확인하세요. 이후 밝혀진 전체 왜곡 규모는 약 110억 달러로 알려져 있습니다. 카드에는 'about $11 billion'으로 적었습니다.
계산 확인 (가상): 매출 $10.0M − 비용 $9.5M = 이익 $0.5M. $1.0M을 5년 자산으로 바꾸면 올해 비용 = $9.5M − $1.0M + $0.2M = $8.7M, 이익 = $1.3M. 현금 지출은 두 경우 모두 동일.
교육훈련비와 광고비는 국제회계기준과 미국 회계기준 모두에서 일반적으로 발생 시점에 비용으로 처리합니다. 소프트웨어 개발비는 조건을 충족하면 일부를 자산으로 기록할 수 있습니다. 특정 국가 세무 기준은 다루지 않았습니다.

cards.title: How WorldCom turned $3.8 billion of phone bills into 'investments'
body: In 2002, WorldCom was one of America's largest phone and internet companies. Then it admitted that about $3.8 billion of ordinary operating costs had been recorded as long-term investments.
Not a single dollar of cash was hidden. The company only changed one label, and that turned losses into reported profits.

image.label: A stack of bills relabeled as a building block
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 'Bills'라고 적힌 영수증 더미에 누군가 'Investment' 라벨을 덧붙이는 장면. 뒤쪽에 전화선과 통신탑 실루엣. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which spending is an asset?
body: You run the operations team inside a large manufacturer. This quarter your team spent $50,000 three different ways. Finance asks which one should be recorded as an asset rather than a cost of this quarter.

options.text: $50,000 of repairs that keep old machines running
options.feedback: Repairs keep things working as they were. They don't add future benefit, so they count as a cost of this period.

options.text: $50,000 for a new machine that will run for five years
options.feedback: The machine will keep producing for years and the company owns it. That future benefit is what makes spending an asset.

options.text: $50,000 for a training program that will help the team for years
options.feedback: Good instinct about future benefit. But staff can leave and the benefit is hard to measure, so training is usually recorded as a cost right away.

cards.title: Costs used up today, booked as if they lasted years.
body: WorldCom paid other phone companies to carry its customers' calls on their networks. These **line costs** were used up the moment the calls went through.

Instead of recording them as costs, staff moved them into the account for long-term equipment. Profit jumped. A small internal audit team, led by Cynthia Cooper, traced the entries and raised the alarm.
The company filed for bankruptcy within weeks. The total misstatement eventually grew to about $11 billion.

cards.title: Assets vs expenses
body: An **asset** is spending that will keep benefiting the business in future periods, and that the business controls. An **expense** is spending that is used up now.
The test is simple: will this still be working for us next year? A new oven, a delivery van or a warehouse lease deposit, yes. Electricity, rent for this month or a repair, no.
Assets sit on the balance sheet and their cost is spread over the years they help. Expenses reduce this period's profit in full.

image.label: Spending split into two paths: this year vs future years
image.brief: 동전 더미가 두 갈래 길로 나뉘는 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Expense: used up now'는 올해 달력 한 장으로, 오른쪽 'Asset: helps for years'는 여러 해 달력에 조금씩 나뉘어 들어감.

cards.title: Same cash, different profit.
body: A business has $10M in sales and $9.5M in costs. It moves $1M of those costs into assets, spread over five years. This year it records only $0.2M of that $1M. Profit **more than doubles** and cash doesn't change at all.

cards.title: Inside companies, the label decides whose budget pays.
body: Many companies keep two budgets: one for **capital spending** on assets, one for running costs. A team that has used up its running budget is tempted to call a repair an "upgrade".
That isn't fraud on WorldCom's scale. But it hides the real cost of running the team and makes this year look cheaper than it was.
cards.softwareNote: Accounting rules can allow part of the cost of building software to be recorded as an asset. That is legitimate, but a company that records more developer time as an asset shows higher profit than one that records it all as cost.

cards.title: The reverse mistake costs too.
body: Recording real investments as expenses makes a good year look bad, and can scare off a lender or a buyer. It also hides how much the business owns.
Many businesses set a small threshold and simply expense anything below it. That keeps the books simple.
And an asset is only as real as its future benefit. A machine that no longer works is not worth what you paid for it.

cards.title: Now it's a chain of 12 stores.
body: This year you spent $80,000 on new refrigerated display cases that should last eight years, $80,000 on repainting and deep cleaning, and $80,000 on a holiday ad campaign. You're preparing numbers for the bank. What do you record as assets?

options.feedback: You own them and they'll sell product for years. Profit looks lower now, but the bank sees numbers it can trust.

options.text: The display cases and the ad campaign, because the brand lasts
options.feedback: Ads may help for a while, but the benefit can't be measured or controlled, so they're normally treated as an expense. Counting them inflates this year's profit.

options.text: All three, to show the bank a stronger year
options.feedback: Profit would rise by most of $160,000 on paper with no extra cash. If the bank notices, you lose its trust along with the loan.

cards.title: Ask whether spending will still be working next year.
body: If yes, it's an asset and its cost is spread over time. If no, it's an expense today. The label moves profit between years, never cash.
**Try it today:** list your five biggest purchases this year. Mark each one: still helping us next year, or used up already?
